Goodness, no, I don't think I'm worried. Well, I mean, I worry about normal things. Bills? Oh heavens, no. I pay my bills the very day they come in the mail. I still write paper checks, you know. My daughter is always pestering me to do it on the iPad, but I just don't trust it. Just big gray blobs floating in the water. I asked the clerk—it was a new girl, not Susan. Susan retired to Florida last year to be near her sister who had that terrible hip replacement. Anyway, I asked the new girl if they had any nice flowers or flags, and she just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Young people today just don't appreciate a pretty piece of mail. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, keeping up with things. No, I don't have any trouble. I write all my doctor appointments on the big calendar on the fridge, right next to the grocery list. And my medications are all sorted in one of those plastic boxes with the little lids that snap shut for the days of the week. Though the 'T' and the 'W' are starting to rub off on mine... I should probably get a new one. Maybe I'll ask David to drive me to the pharmacy later.

Oh, let's see... no, I don't think I take anything at all. No prescriptions, no. I've always been very healthy, praise the Lord. My mother was the same way, you know. She lived to be ninety-two and never took so much as an aspirin. She swore by a hot cup of lemon water every morning and a brisk walk. \n\nWe used to walk down to the bakery on Elm Street. Oh, the smell of that place! They made these little almond cookies that were just heavenly. The baker, Mr. Rossi, was this big, booming Italian man who always wore a white apron covered in flour. He had a parrot in the shop, if you can believe it. A bright green thing that would squawk \"Fresh bread! Fresh bread!\" whenever the bell above the door rang. I always wondered if it was sanitary, having a bird right there near the pastries, but nobody seemed to mind back then. Things were so different. \n\nNow, you go into a bakery and everything is wrapped in plastic, and the girls behind the counter look at their phones the whole time. It's just a shame. But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, pills. No, I don't take any. Just a daily vitamin, maybe, when I remember to buy them. But no real medicine. I just have all this pep!\n\nDoctor: Does this restless, need-to-move feeling mainly involve your legs, and does it tend to get worse in the evening or when you're sitting still, then feel better once you get up and move around?\n\nPatient: My legs? Pat Sajak, he's always so charming. Though I do think Vanna White's dresses have gotten a bit too flashy lately. Back in the eighties, she wore such elegant gowns. My sister Margaret had a dress just like one Vanna wore in 1986—a lovely emerald green silk with a sweetheart neckline. She wore it to her daughter's wedding. \n\nOh, that wedding! It was in this beautiful old church with stained glass windows that looked like spun sugar when the sun hit them. But the reception, well, they had a chocolate fountain. A fountain! Can you imagine? Some little boy stuck his whole hand right in it and then wiped it on the white linen tablecloths. His mother was mortified. She was wearing this awful peach pantsuit that just washed her right out. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Sad? Oh, heavens no. I haven't been sad at all. If anything, I'm just too full of beans! I haven't lost interest in anything, either. I still love my gardening. I was just out there this morning pulling up weeds around the hydrangeas. 

Hydrangeas are such funny plants, aren't they? You know, you can change the color of the blooms just by putting things in the soil. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house on the corner with the terrible vinyl siding—she puts rusty nails in her soil to make her hydrangeas blue! I told her that sounds like a good way to get lockjaw if you aren't careful with your trowel, but she swears by it. I prefer pink, myself. Pink is such a cheerful color. I had a pink sweater set in the fifties that was just darling. It had these little pearl buttons down the front. I wore it when I met my husband, actually! We were at a church picnic, and he was trying to carry three plates of potato salad at once. 

He dropped one right on my nice white Keds! But he was so apologetic, and he had the bluest eyes... just like Paul Newman. Did you ever see that movie with Paul Newman, the one with the bicycles? Or was it cars? He liked cars, didn't he? He had his own salad dressing, too. I buy the vinaigrette sometimes, it's very tangy. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my mood. No, no, I'm not down in the dumps at all. I just can't seem to stop going and going and going!

It was in this beautiful old church with stained glass windows that looked like spun sugar when the sun hit them. But the reception, well, they had a chocolate fountain. A fountain! Can you imagine? Some little boy stuck his whole hand right in it and then wiped it on the white linen tablecloths. His mother was mortified. She was wearing this awful peach pantsuit that just washed her right out. Peach is such a hard color to wear. You really need the right complexion for it. \n\nBut anyway, what was I saying? Oh, moving around. Yes, getting up doesn't really make it go away. I just feel like I need to be doing something constantly. Even when I'm up and walking, I'm tapping my fingers or humming a tune. It's just a constant buzzing feeling everywhere!\n\nDoctor: Over the past year, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy—along with this restless feeling?\n\nPatient: Sad? You know, you can change the color of the blooms just by putting things in the soil. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house on the corner with the terrible vinyl siding—she puts rusty nails in her soil to make her hydrangeas blue! I told her that sounds like a good way to get lockjaw if you aren't careful with your trowel, but she swears by it. I prefer pink, myself. Pink is such a cheerful color. I had a pink sweater set in the fifties that was just darling. It had these little pearl buttons down the front. I wore it when I met my husband, actually! We were at a church picnic, and he was trying to carry three plates of potato salad at once. \n\nHe dropped one right on my nice white Keds! But he was so apologetic, and he had the bluest eyes... just like Paul Newman. Did you ever see that movie with Paul Newman, the one with the bicycles? Or was it cars? He liked cars, didn't he? He had his own salad dressing, too. I buy the vinaigrette sometimes, it's very tangy. \n\nBut anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my mood. No, no, I'm not down in the dumps at all. Racing thoughts? Well, I don't know if I'd say racing, exactly. I mean, my mind is always busy, of course. There's always something to think about! Like this morning, I was thinking about whether I should make a pot roast for Sunday dinner. 

A good pot roast takes time, you know. You have to sear the meat first to lock in the juices. My mother taught me that. She used this heavy cast-iron skillet that weighed an absolute ton. I don't know how she lifted it, she was such a tiny woman! Barely five feet tall in her stocking feet. She used to buy her shoes in the children's department because her feet were so small. They had these little Mary Janes with a strap across the top... I always wanted a pair like that, but my feet were too wide. 

I had to wear these clunky oxfords when I was a girl. They were so sturdy, they felt like wearing bricks! But my father insisted. He said you needed good arch support or your feet would fall flat as pancakes by the time you were thirty. He was a podiatrist, you see. Dr. Arthur Pendleton. Everyone in town went to him for their corns and bunions. He had this big jar of peppermints on his desk for the children, but they were those chalky ones that tasted like toothpaste. I always preferred butterscotch, myself. Those little yellow candies wrapped in cellophane... they just melt in your mouth! 

But what were we talking about? Oh, my mind jumping around. Well, I suppose I do think about a lot of things, but I wouldn't say my thoughts are racing or out of control. I'm just... thinking! There's just so much to remember, isn't there?

Fixing things, arranging the pantry, volunteering for just one more thing at the church... even at 87, I have a terrible time just sitting down and being still. \n\nIt’s funny, I was trying to watch Jeopardy last night—I still miss Alex Trebek, you know, he had such a comforting voice. My late husband and I used to watch him every single evening on this dreadful green floral sofa we bought at a Sears back in the eighties. That Sears is a mattress store now, if you can believe it. They just tear everything down these days. But anyway, I couldn't even sit through Final Jeopardy without getting up to dust the mantelpiece! I just always have to be doing something, and my daughter thought maybe I should talk to someone about it.\n\nDoctor: When you feel like you can't sit still, is it because you're feeling worried or anxious about something, or more because you're feeling unusually energetic, upbeat, or 'wired'?\n\nPatient: Goodness, no, I don't think I'm worried. Well, I mean, I worry about normal things. Like my grandson, David—he just bought one of those electric scooters, and I read in the Sunday paper that the batteries on those things can just catch fire! Can you imagine? Just bursting into flames right there in the garage. I told my daughter she needs to make him keep it outside, but she never listens to me. She gets that stubbornness from her father's side, bless his heart. \n\nBut no, it's not worry that makes me get up and dust the mantel. And I certainly wouldn't say I'm \"wired\" or unusually energetic. I'm 87! I haven't been wired since... well, maybe when they used to put real sugar in Coca-Cola. Oh, the little glass bottles were so much better, weren't they? Now everything is plastic and it just tastes like a factory. I stopped drinking it altogether in the nineties. \n\nBut anyway, what was I... oh, right. No, I don't feel anxious or upbeat when it happens. I just... I don't really know why I do it. I just feel like my hands and feet need to be busy, even when I'm perfectly content.\n\nDoctor: Have you or your family noticed any recent problems with your memory—like forgetting recent conversations, misplacing things more often, or getting confused about dates or directions?\n\nPatient: Well, memory... no, I wouldn't say my memory is going. I mean, my daughter hasn't said anything about it. She's always so quick to point out if I've done something wrong, you know. Just last week, she came over and saw I had reorganized the spice rack alphabetically instead of by cuisine, and she made this little huffing sound. She does that exact same huff her father used to do when I'd suggest we stop and ask for directions. \n\nWe took this trip to Mount Rushmore back in '76—the bicentennial year, you know. Everyone was wearing those awful polyester pantsuits in red, white, and blue. I had a lovely navy one, actually, with little anchor buttons. But anyway, he refused to pull over in South Dakota, and we ended up at some roadside attraction with a giant prairie dog made of concrete. It was the strangest thing. I just have a lot of energy, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any recent weight loss, feeling unusually warm or sweaty, or a racing heartbeat lately?\n\nPatient: Weight loss? Oh, heavens no. If anything, I've put on a pound or two since the holidays. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house with the hydrangeas that always look a bit wilted—she brought over this fruitcake. Now, normally I can't stand fruitcake. It's just heavy and tastes like old perfume. But hers had these little candied cherries that reminded me of the ones my mother used to put in her icebox cookies. \n\nWe used to have this big, clunky Frigidaire when I was a girl. The handle was so heavy you had to use two hands to pull it open. My brother Tommy once got his tie caught in the door right before church. Oh, he was so mad! I don't know why boys wear such ugly things when they're teenagers. \n\nBut no, I'm not losing weight. And I haven't been sweaty or had my heart race, either. My heart is just fine. They squeeze your arm so tight I always think it's going to pop right off like a doll's arm. But no, none of that. I just can't sit still!\n\nDoctor: Have you or your daughter noticed any new difficulty keeping up with things like paying bills, managing your medications, or remembering appointments?\n\nPatient: Bills? Oh heavens, no. I pay my bills the very day they come in the mail. I still write paper checks, you know. My daughter is always pestering me to do it on the iPad, but I just don't trust it. The internet is just floating around in the air, it feels like anyone could just reach up and grab your bank account right out of the sky! I like to sit at my kitchen table with a good pen. I only use blue ink. Black ink always looks so severe, like a collection notice. \n\nI went to the post office just Tuesday to get a new book of stamps for my envelopes, and they gave me these ones with... oh, what were they... sea cows! Susan retired to Florida last year to be near her sister who had that terrible hip replacement. I should probably get a new one. Maybe I'll ask David to drive me to the pharmacy later. \n\nBut no, no trouble at all with my memory or my chores. I'm sharp as a tack! I just have these fidgety hands and feet that want to be doing something.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me about all the medications you're currently taking, including any new prescriptions or over-the-counter drugs you started in the past year?\n\nPatient: Medications? Oh, let's see... no, I don't think I take anything at all. No prescriptions, no. I've always been very healthy, praise the Lord. My mother was the same way, you know. She lived to be ninety-two and never took so much as an aspirin. She swore by a hot cup of lemon water every morning and a brisk walk. \n\nWe used to walk down to the bakery on Elm Street. Oh, the smell of that place! They made these little almond cookies that were just heavenly. The baker, Mr. Rossi, was this big, booming Italian man who always wore a white apron covered in flour. I just have all this pep!\n\nDoctor: Does this restless, need-to-move feeling mainly involve your legs, and does it tend to get worse in the evening or when you're sitting still, then feel better once you get up and move around?\n\nPatient: My legs? Oh, no, it's not just my legs. It's my hands, my arms, my whole body just feels like a motor is running inside me! I don't know about the evening... I feel like this all day long, really. Sitting still is just impossible, whether it's morning, noon, or night. \n\nLike yesterday, I was trying to sit and watch that nice game show, the one with the spinning wheel? Pat Sajak, he's always so charming. Though I do think Vanna White's dresses have gotten a bit too flashy lately. Back in the eighties, she wore such elegant gowns. My sister Margaret had a dress just like one Vanna wore in 1986—a lovely emerald green silk with a sweetheart neckline. She wore it to her daughter's wedding. \n\nOh, that wedding! It was in this beautiful old church with stained glass windows that looked like spun sugar when the sun hit them. But the reception, well, they had a chocolate fountain. A fountain! Can you imagine? Some little boy stuck his whole hand right in it and then wiped it on the white linen tablecloths. His mother was mortified. She was wearing this awful peach pantsuit that just washed her right out. Peach is such a hard color to wear. You really need the right complexion for it. \n\nBut anyway, what was I saying? Oh, moving around. Yes, getting up doesn't really make it go away. I just feel like I need to be doing something constantly. Even when I'm up and walking, I'm tapping my fingers or humming a tune. It's just a constant buzzing feeling everywhere!\n\nDoctor: Over the past year, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy—along with this restless feeling?\n\nPatient: Sad? Oh, heavens no. I haven't been sad at all. If anything, I'm just too full of beans! I haven't lost interest in anything, either. I still love my gardening. I was just out there this morning pulling up weeds around the hydrangeas. \n\nHydrangeas are such funny plants, aren't they? You know, you can change the color of the blooms just by putting things in the soil. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house on the corner with the terrible vinyl siding—she puts rusty nails in her soil to make her hydrangeas blue! I told her that sounds like a good way to get lockjaw if you aren't careful with your trowel, but she swears by it. I prefer pink, myself. Pink is such a cheerful color. We were at a church picnic, and he was trying to carry three plates of potato salad at once. \n\nHe dropped one right on my nice white Keds! But he was so apologetic, and he had the bluest eyes... just like Paul Newman. Did you ever see that movie with Paul Newman, the one with the bicycles? Or was it cars? He liked cars, didn't he? He had his own salad dressing, too. I buy the vinaigrette sometimes, it's very tangy. \n\nBut anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my mood. No, no, I'm not down in the dumps at all. I just can't seem to stop going and going and going!\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed any change in how much sleep you need—like feeling fully rested after only four or five hours, or finding you just don't need as much sleep as you used to?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Everyone in town went to him for their corns and bunions. He had this big jar of peppermints on his desk for the children, but they were those chalky ones that tasted like toothpaste. I should probably get a new one. Maybe I'll ask David to drive me to the pharmacy later. \n\nBut no, no trouble at all with my memory or my chores. I'm sharp as a tack! I just have these fidgety hands and feet that want to be doing something.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me about all the medications you're currently taking, including any new prescriptions or over-the-counter drugs you started in the past year?\n\nPatient: Medications? Oh, let's see... no, I don't think I take anything at all. No prescriptions, no. I've always been very healthy, praise the Lord. My mother was the same way, you know. She lived to be ninety-two and never took so much as an aspirin. She swore by a hot cup of lemon water every morning and a brisk walk. \n\nWe used to walk down to the bakery on Elm Street. Oh, the smell of that place! They made these little almond cookies that were just heavenly. The baker, Mr. Rossi, was this big, booming Italian man who always wore a white apron covered in flour. He had a parrot in the shop, if you can believe it. A bright green thing that would squawk \"Fresh bread! Fresh bread!\" whenever the bell above the door rang. I always wondered if it was sanitary, having a bird right there near the pastries, but nobody seemed to mind back then. Things were so different. \n\nNow, you go into a bakery and everything is wrapped in plastic, and the girls behind the counter look at their phones the whole time. It's just a shame. But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, pills. No, I don't take any. Just a daily vitamin, maybe, when I remember to buy them. But no real medicine. I just have all this pep!\n\nDoctor: Does this restless, need-to-move feeling mainly involve your legs, and does it tend to get worse in the evening or when you're sitting still, then feel better once you get up and move around?\n\nPatient: My legs? Oh, no, it's not just my legs. It's my hands, my arms, my whole body just feels like a motor is running inside me! I don't know about the evening... I feel like this all day long, really. Sitting still is just impossible, whether it's morning, noon, or night. \n\nLike yesterday, I was trying to sit and watch that nice game show, the one with the spinning wheel? Pat Sajak, he's always so charming. Though I do think Vanna White's dresses have gotten a bit too flashy lately. Back in the eighties, she wore such elegant gowns. My sister Margaret had a dress just like one Vanna wore in 1986—a lovely emerald green silk with a sweetheart neckline. She wore it to her daughter's wedding. \n\nOh, that wedding! It was in this beautiful old church with stained glass windows that looked like spun sugar when the sun hit them. But the reception, well, they had a chocolate fountain. A fountain! Can you imagine? Some little boy stuck his whole hand right in it and then wiped it on the white linen tablecloths. His mother was mortified. She was wearing this awful peach pantsuit that just washed her right out. Peach is such a hard color to wear. You really need the right complexion for it. \n\nBut anyway, what was I saying? Oh, moving around. Yes, getting up doesn't really make it go away. I just feel like I need to be doing something constantly. Even when I'm up and walking, I'm tapping my fingers or humming a tune. It's just a constant buzzing feeling everywhere!\n\nDoctor: Over the past year, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy—along with this restless feeling?\n\nPatient: Sad? You know, you can change the color of the blooms just by putting things in the soil. I had a pink sweater set in the fifties that was just darling. It had these little pearl buttons down the front. I wore it when I met my husband, actually! We were at a church picnic, and he was trying to carry three plates of potato salad at once. \n\nHe dropped one right on my nice white Keds! I like to be in bed by ten o'clock sharp, right after the local news. \n\nThe news is so depressing these days, though, isn't it? It's all just crime and politics. She used real tart cherries, not that syrupy canned stuff. You have to use the tart ones or it's just too sweet. She won a blue ribbon at the state fair for it in 1974. Or was it '75? No, it was '74 because that was the year we had that terrible blizzard and we were snowed in for three days! We just sat around playing Pinochle and eating cherry pie. I don't wake up feeling like I only need four hours or anything like that.
